definition: A metal strip across the guitar's neck; each one raises a string by a semitone.
The front of the guitar's neck, where the strings are pressed against the frets.
The slotted bar at the headstock end of the neck that holds the strings; it acts as fret 0.
The vibrating length of an open string, from nut to saddle (about 648 mm on a Fender, 628 mm on a Gibson).
A magnet and coil under an electric guitar's strings that turns their vibration into an electrical signal.
The usual guitar tuning, low to high E2 A2 D3 G3 B3 E4: fourths apart except G–B, a major third.
Standard tuning with the low E string lowered a whole step to D.
An open, suspended-sounding tuning (D A D G A D) used in Celtic and modal playing.
A tuning in which the open strings sound a chord, as in open G (D G D G B D).
A clamp across all strings at one fret that moves the nut up, so chord shapes sound higher.
Guitar notation with one line per string and fret numbers on the lines.
A picture of the neck showing where to put the fingers for a chord; also written as six characters such as x32010.
Picking single notes with strictly alternating down and up strokes.
Plucking the strings with the thumb and fingers rather than a pick.
Sounding a note by bringing a fretting finger down hard on the string without picking; a pull-off plucks the string as the finger leaves.
Pushing a string sideways across the fret to raise its pitch, often by a half or whole step.
Resting the side of the picking hand on the strings by the bridge for a short, chunky tone.
A bell-like tone made by touching a string lightly over the 12th, 7th or 5th fret and picking it.
Where the fretting hand sits on the neck, named by the fret under the first finger.
A fixed fingering that finds the same note an octave higher on another string.
One of five one-position fingerings of the pentatonic scale that together cover the neck.
Scale fingerings with exactly three notes on each string.
A way of mapping the neck with five movable shapes taken from the open C, A, G, E and D chords.
A movable chord in which the first finger presses all the strings at one fret.
A chord in the first few frets that uses open strings.
Root and fifth (often with the octave) without a third, written C5; the core of rock guitar.
A seventh-chord voicing made by dropping the second-highest note of a close-position chord down an octave (drop-3: the third-highest).
A three-note voicing of root, third and seventh.
A group of adjacent strings used for a voicing, such as the top three (G B E).
Chord charts written with scale-degree numbers instead of chord letters, so they work in any key.
The descending progression i–♭VII–♭VI–V (Am–G–F–E), common in flamenco and rock.
A swung rhythm, and on guitar the alternating root-fifth/root-sixth bass pattern of blues and early rock.
The notes of a chord played one after another.
A chord tone that an improvised line aims to land on, usually on a strong beat.
